tips.title: IPMAT, then C
tips.body: **I**nterphase, **P**rophase, **M**etaphase, **A**naphase, **T**elophase — then **C**ytokinesis. The specification names all six, and questions ask for them in order, so the mnemonic earns its keep.

tips.title: Two identical diploid cells, or it is meiosis
tips.body: Mitosis gives **two** cells, **genetically identical**, **diploid**. If an answer has **four** cells or **half** the chromosomes, it has described **meiosis** — which is a different process for a different purpose.

tips.title: The DNA is copied in interphase
tips.body: Before the division starts, not during it. By the time the chromosomes line up in metaphase, each already has its copy attached — which is why pulling them apart gives two complete sets.

tips.title: Plants elongate, animals do not
tips.body: Animal growth is **division and differentiation**; plant growth is **division, elongation and differentiation**. Elongation is the one extra process, and it is what the comparison question is testing.

tips.title: On a percentile chart, the change is the point
tips.body: Being on the 9th percentile is not a problem if the child has always been there. **Crossing several lines** is what matters. Answers that judge the number rather than the trend miss what the chart is for.

why.matters:
You started as one cell. Everything you are made of came from that cell dividing, and the remarkable part is not the number but the **fidelity**: each division has to give two cells with an identical set of chromosomes, or the copy is wrong from then on.

So mitosis is a copying process with checks, and this topic is what happens when it works — growth, repair, whole organisms from cuttings — and what happens when the control over it fails.

examples.title: Why twenty divisions is a million cells
examples.body:
Mitosis doubles. One cell becomes two, two become four, and the number climbs in a way that is hard to feel: after **10** divisions there are **1 024** cells, and after **20** there are over **1 million**.

That is how an embryo is built and how a cut closes over. It is also why a mistake in the control of division matters so much: a cell that divides when it should not does not make one extra cell, it makes a line of them that goes on doubling.

props.caption: Cells after each number of divisions, to scale

visual.alt: Three bars drawn to true scale showing how mitosis doubles: two cells after one division, one thousand and twenty-four after ten, and over a million after twenty

examples.title: Why cancer is a fault in the timing, not in the cell
examples.body:
Cancer cells are not invaders and they are not usually doing anything exotic. They are the body's own cells **dividing when they should have stopped** — the control over mitosis has failed, and the result is a mass of cells where there should be none.

That is why the risk factors in the earlier topic matter here: things that damage DNA, such as tobacco smoke or ultraviolet light, damage the genes that do the controlling. And it is why *uncontrolled cell division* is the phrase worth having — the process is normal, and only the control is broken.

visual.alt: A table contrasting normal cell division, which happens when more cells are needed and stops when they are not, with cancer, where the cells divide without that control and a tumour forms

examples.title: What a percentile chart is really showing
examples.body:
A baby on the 9th percentile is not unwell. It means nine babies in a hundred of that age are smaller — somebody has to be there, and that child has probably been there all along.

What a nurse is watching for is the **shape of the line**, not its height. A child who tracks the same percentile for two years is growing normally, whatever the number. A child who **crosses several lines** in a few months is the one worth investigating, in either direction. It is one of the clearest cases in the course of a measurement whose meaning is in its change.

visual.alt: Three percentile lines rising with age on a growth chart, the ninth, fiftieth and ninety-first, showing that a child tracking any one of them is growing normally and that crossing several is what matters

steps.title: Mitosis and the cell cycle
steps.body:
**Mitosis** is how body cells divide. It produces **two daughter cells**, each with an **identical set of chromosomes** to the parent cell — so the two new cells are **genetically identical** to each other and to the cell they came from, and both are **diploid** body cells.

Mitosis is one part of a longer **cell cycle**, and the specification names the stages:

1. **Interphase** — the cell **grows**, the **DNA replicates** so each chromosome is copied, and the organelles are duplicated. This is the longest stage.
2. **Prophase** — the chromosomes **condense** and become visible; the nuclear membrane **breaks down**.
3. **Metaphase** — the chromosomes **line up** across the middle of the cell.
4. **Anaphase** — the copies are **pulled apart** to opposite ends of the cell.
5. **Telophase** — a **nuclear membrane forms** around each set of chromosomes.
6. **Cytokinesis** — the **cytoplasm and cell membrane divide**, giving two separate cells.

The first letters spell **IPMAT**, with **C** for cytokinesis at the end.

One point of order that matters: the DNA is copied in **interphase**, **before** the division begins. By the time the chromosomes line up, every one already has its copy attached — which is why pulling them apart gives two complete sets.

steps.title: Why mitosis matters
steps.body:
The specification names **three** reasons an organism needs mitosis, and a question asking for its importance wants them:

- **Growth.** A multicellular organism gets larger by making **more cells**, not by making its cells larger. An adult human has vastly more cells than a baby, and they arose by mitosis.
- **Repair.** Damaged or worn-out cells are replaced with identical ones. Skin, gut lining and blood cells are replaced constantly.
- **Asexual reproduction.** Some organisms produce offspring from a single parent by mitosis. The offspring are **genetically identical** to the parent — clones.

All three depend on the same property: mitosis produces cells **identical** to the original. For repair that is essential — a replacement skin cell must be a skin cell. For asexual reproduction it is the defining feature.

It is also why mitosis is **not** how gametes are made. Sex cells need **half** the chromosomes and need to differ from one another, which is a different process entirely.

steps.title: Cancer
steps.body:
Cell division is normally **controlled**: cells divide when more are needed and stop when they are not.

**Cancer is the result of changes in cells that lead to uncontrolled cell division.** The cells keep dividing when they should have stopped, and the mass of cells that builds up is a **tumour**.

That single sentence is the specification's definition, and the word that carries it is **uncontrolled**. Cancer is not a different kind of cell division; it is **ordinary mitosis that has lost its controls**.

What follows from that:

- A tumour grows because cells are being **added faster than they are lost**.
- Some tumours stay in one place; in others, cells break away and spread through the blood or lymph to form tumours elsewhere.
- Anything that **damages the DNA controlling cell division** raises the risk — which is why ionising radiation, ultraviolet light and carcinogens in tobacco smoke are risk factors.

So the connection to the rest of this topic is direct: mitosis is essential and happens constantly, and cancer is what happens when its controls fail.

steps.title: Growth and differentiation
steps.body:
**Growth** is a permanent increase in size, and the specification splits it by kingdom because the processes differ.

**In animals**, growth involves:

- **cell division** — more cells, by mitosis
- **differentiation** — cells becoming specialised

**In plants**, growth involves:

- **cell division**
- **elongation** — cells getting **longer**, mainly by taking in water so the vacuole enlarges
- **differentiation**

So a plant does everything an animal does **plus elongation**. That is the examinable difference, and it explains why a plant can grow rapidly upwards without making many new cells: the existing ones stretch.

**Differentiation** is the process by which a cell becomes **specialised** for a particular job — developing a structure that suits its function. A red blood cell loses its nucleus to carry more haemoglobin; a nerve cell grows long to carry impulses; a root hair cell grows a long extension to increase surface area.

**Why differentiation matters** (spec point 2.6): a multicellular organism can only work if different cells do different jobs. Without it every cell would be identical and could do nothing specialised — no carrying oxygen, no transmitting impulses, no absorbing water efficiently.

In animals, most cells differentiate **early** and then lose the ability. In plants, cells can differentiate **throughout life**, which is why a cutting can grow into a whole new plant.

steps.title: Percentile charts, and stem cells
steps.body:
**Percentile charts** are used to monitor growth in babies and children. A chart plots mass, length or head circumference against age, with curved lines showing percentiles.

A child on the **75th percentile** for mass is **heavier than 75%** of children of that age — and lighter than the other 25%.

The key idea, and the one questions test: **which percentile a child is on matters far less than whether they stay on it.** A child who has always been on the 25th percentile is growing normally. A child who **crosses several percentile lines downwards** may have a problem, even if they are still in a normal range — because their growth has changed relative to other children.

**Stem cells** are undifferentiated cells that can divide and then **differentiate** into other types. The specification names three:

- **Embryonic stem cells** — from an early embryo. They can differentiate into **any** type of cell.
- **Stem cells in animals**, found in places such as bone marrow. These can differentiate into a **limited range** of types — bone marrow stem cells produce blood cells.
- **Meristems in plants** — at the tips of roots and shoots. Plant meristem cells can differentiate into **any** plant cell type, and can do so **throughout the plant's life**.

That last difference is why a cutting from a plant can grow into a complete new plant, while a piece of an animal cannot.

steps.title: Going deeper: stem cells, benefits and risks
steps.body:
Spec point 2.9 asks you to **discuss** the benefits and risks of using stem cells in medicine, which means giving both and reaching a view.

**The benefits.** Stem cells could **replace cells that have been damaged or lost**, which no drug can do:

- **Type 1 diabetes** — replacing the insulin-producing cells of the pancreas.
- **Paralysis** — replacing damaged nerve cells in the spinal cord.
- **Blood disorders and some cancers** — bone marrow transplants already do this, and are the established case that shows the principle works.
- Stem cells can also be used to **grow tissue for testing new drugs**, reducing the need for animal testing.

**The risks and objections.**

- **Rejection.** Cells from a donor may be attacked by the patient's immune system, so immunosuppressants are needed — unless the patient's own cells are used.
- **Infection.** Any transfer of cells carries a risk of introducing a virus.
- **Uncontrolled division.** Stem cells divide readily, and cells that keep dividing when they should stop form **tumours** — the link back to cancer in this same topic.
- **Ethical objections** to **embryonic** stem cells, because obtaining them destroys an embryo. People disagree about the moral status of an embryo at that stage, and that disagreement is not a scientific question.

**How to discuss it well.** Notice that the **objections apply differently to different sources**. The ethical objection applies to **embryonic** stem cells; using a patient's **own adult** stem cells avoids both it and rejection — but adult stem cells can become a **narrower range** of cell types, so they cannot treat everything. The trade-off is therefore **between usefulness and acceptability**, and saying that is worth more than listing benefits against risks.

**Three points of precision.**

- **Mitosis makes two identical daughter cells.** If your answer has four cells, or cells with half the chromosomes, you have described **meiosis**.
- **The DNA replicates in interphase**, before the stages of mitosis proper. A question asking when the DNA is copied has a specific answer.
- **Cancer is uncontrolled division**, not division that is somehow faulty in kind. The word *uncontrolled* is the mark.

And on **percentile charts**: the examiners are consistently interested in **crossing lines**, not in the number. A child on the 2nd percentile who has always been there is growing normally; a child falling from the 50th to the 9th is the one to look at.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Mitosis** produces **two daughter cells**, each with an **identical set of chromosomes** to the parent: **genetically identical diploid** body cells.
- The cell cycle: **interphase, prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase, cytokinesis** — IPMAT, then C.
- The **DNA replicates in interphase**, **before** the division begins.
- Mitosis is needed for **growth, repair and asexual reproduction**.
- **Cancer** is the result of changes in cells leading to **uncontrolled cell division**; the mass that builds up is a **tumour**.
- **Growth in animals**: cell division and **differentiation**.
- **Growth in plants**: cell division, **elongation** and differentiation — elongation is the extra one.
- **Differentiation** is a cell becoming **specialised**, with a structure that suits its function.
- **Percentile charts**: a child on the 75th percentile is heavier than 75% of children that age. **Crossing several lines matters; the number itself does not.**
- **Embryonic stem cells** can become **any** cell type; **adult stem cells** in animals a **limited range**; **meristems** in plants **any plant cell**, throughout life.
- **Benefits**: replacing damaged cells, treating diabetes and paralysis, testing drugs.
- **Risks**: rejection, infection, uncontrolled division forming tumours, and ethical objections to using embryos.

questions.prompt: Describe the stages of the cell cycle, state what mitosis produces, and explain why mitosis is important to a multicellular organism.
questions.solution: The cell cycle begins with interphase, which is the longest stage. During interphase the cell grows, the DNA replicates so that each chromosome is copied, and the organelles are duplicated. Mitosis then follows. In prophase the chromosomes condense so that they become visible and the nuclear membrane breaks down. In metaphase the chromosomes line up across the middle of the cell. In anaphase the copies of each chromosome are pulled apart to opposite ends of the cell. In telophase a nuclear membrane forms around each of the two sets of chromosomes. Finally, in cytokinesis, the cytoplasm and the cell membrane divide, producing two separate cells. Mitosis produces two daughter cells, each with an identical set of chromosomes to the parent cell, so they are genetically identical diploid body cells. It is important because it allows an organism to grow by producing more cells, to repair itself by replacing damaged or worn out cells with identical ones, and in some organisms to reproduce asexually, producing offspring that are genetically identical to the parent.

questions.modelAnswer:
**The cell cycle, in order.**

1. **Interphase** — the longest stage. The cell **grows**, the **DNA replicates** so each chromosome is copied, and the organelles are duplicated.
2. **Prophase** — the chromosomes **condense** and become visible; the nuclear membrane **breaks down**.
3. **Metaphase** — the chromosomes **line up** across the middle.
4. **Anaphase** — the copies are **pulled apart** to opposite ends.
5. **Telophase** — a **nuclear membrane forms** around each set.
6. **Cytokinesis** — the **cytoplasm and cell membrane divide**, giving two cells.

**What it produces.** **Two** daughter cells, each with an **identical set of chromosomes** to the parent: **genetically identical diploid** body cells.

**Why it matters.**

- **Growth** — an organism gets larger by making more cells.
- **Repair** — damaged or worn cells are replaced with identical ones.
- **Asexual reproduction** — offspring genetically identical to the single parent.

All three depend on the daughter cells being **identical**, which is exactly what mitosis guarantees — and why it is not how gametes are made.

questions.prompt: Discuss the potential benefits and risks of using stem cells in medicine, referring to both embryonic and adult stem cells.
questions.solution: Stem cells are undifferentiated cells that can divide and then differentiate into other types of cell, which means they could be used to replace cells that have been damaged or lost, something that no drug can do. For example, they might be used to replace the insulin producing cells in the pancreas of a person with type one diabetes, or to replace damaged nerve cells in the spinal cord of someone who is paralysed. Bone marrow transplants already use adult stem cells to treat blood disorders, which shows that the principle works. Stem cells can also be used to grow tissue for testing new drugs, reducing the need for animal testing. There are risks, however. Cells from a donor may be rejected by the patient's immune system, so immunosuppressant drugs would be needed. There is a risk of introducing infection when cells are transferred. Because stem cells divide readily there is a risk that they divide uncontrollably and form tumours. In addition there are ethical objections to the use of embryonic stem cells, because obtaining them destroys an embryo and people disagree about the moral status of an embryo at that stage. Embryonic stem cells can become any type of cell, which makes them the most useful, while adult stem cells taken from the patient's own body avoid both the ethical objection and the risk of rejection, but can only become a limited range of cell types. The decision therefore involves a trade off between how useful the cells are and how acceptable their source is.

questions.modelAnswer:
**The benefits.** Stem cells can **replace cells that have been damaged or lost** — something no drug can do.

- **Type 1 diabetes**: replacing the insulin-producing cells of the pancreas.
- **Paralysis**: replacing damaged nerve cells in the spinal cord.
- **Bone marrow transplants** already work this way, which shows the principle holds.
- Growing tissue for **testing drugs**, reducing animal testing.

**The risks.**

- **Rejection** — the immune system may attack donor cells, so immunosuppressants would be needed.
- **Infection** introduced during the transfer.
- **Uncontrolled division**, forming **tumours** — the same failure of control that defines cancer.

**The ethical objection.** Obtaining **embryonic** stem cells **destroys an embryo**, and people disagree about its moral status. That is not a scientific disagreement, and an answer should say so rather than take a side as though it were.

**The contrast that makes it a discussion.** Embryonic stem cells can become **any** cell type, so they are the most useful. A patient's **own adult** stem cells avoid **both** the ethical objection and the risk of rejection — but can become only a **limited range** of types.

So the choice is a trade-off between **usefulness and acceptability**, which is worth more than a list of benefits set against a list of risks.

examTechnique.body:
Name the stages of the cell cycle in the specification's own order, and include cytokinesis, which is often left off.

When describing what mitosis produces, say two, genetically identical, and diploid. All three words carry marks.

For cancer, use the word uncontrolled. It is the whole definition.

When comparing growth in plants and animals, name elongation as the difference rather than describing both lists in full.

For a percentile chart question, comment on whether the child has stayed on a percentile, not on which one they are on.

When discussing stem cells, give benefits and risks and then distinguish embryonic from adult sources, because the objections apply differently.

Saying the daughter cells have half the chromosomes of the parent.
Saying the DNA is copied during prophase rather than interphase.
Leaving cytokinesis out of the stages.
Saying cancer is cells dividing faster, rather than uncontrolled division.
Judging a percentile chart by the percentile rather than the trend.
Saying adult stem cells can become any type of cell.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer states all three properties of the daughter cells — two, genetically identical, diploid — and so never confuses mitosis with meiosis. It knows the DNA is replicated in interphase and can say why that timing matters. On a percentile chart it comments on the trend, and explains that a child who has always been on a low percentile is growing normally. Discussing stem cells, it separates the ethical objection, which applies to embryonic cells, from the practical limitation of adult cells, and frames the choice as a trade-off between usefulness and acceptability rather than listing pros and cons.
